title: Deterministic Verification and a Single‑Repair Guardrail for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations: a Paired, Shared‑Candidate Study
abstract: We report a preregistered paired experiment that measured how much deterministic validation plus one automated repair (a guarded pipeline) changes verifier-confirmed correctness of the same LLM‑generated configuration candidates versus accepting those candidates as‑is. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics we generated one initial candidate per natural‑language intent (gpt-5-mini) for N=250 paired intents and applied a deterministic network validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) with up to one automated repair on the guarded branch. Results: baseline verifier‑pass 249/250 (99.6%), guarded verifier‑pass 250/250 (100.0%); paired difference = +0.4 percentage points, 95% CI [0.0, 1.2 percentage points], exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. One discordant pair was repaired by the single allowed repair. The preregistered primary hypothesis (expecting ≥15 percentage‑point paired deficit) is not supported. We document the sealed preregistration, shared‑candidate estimand, deterministic execution contract, representative artifacts, and limits on external validity; detailed manifests and analysis artifacts are archived in the execution bundle.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are being proposed to translate operator intent into concrete network configurations, but stochastic generation raises operational correctness concerns. Prior proposals interpose deterministic validators and repair loops (generate–verify–repair, GVR) to detect and correct mechanically checkable errors [refs]. We preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics to quantify the incremental verifier-confirmed benefit of deterministic validation plus one automated repair versus accepting the same raw LLM candidate. The contributions are: (1) a preregistered, artifact-backed paired evaluation using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator on N=250 intent pairs; (2) strict shared_initial_candidate execution and exact paired inference; (3) a near‑null primary result with an evidence-grounded discussion of limitations and next steps.
sections.related_work: Work applying LLMs to intent→configuration and NetOps automation shows LLMs can produce usable draft configurations but frequently require verification or human oversight [10–15]. Architectures that place deterministic checkers and repair loops between stochastic generators and acceptance have been proposed and shown to reduce mechanically verifiable defects in code/configuration domains [2,3,7]. Deterministic network analyzers (Batfish, header‑space approaches, model‑checking toolchains) provide mechanistic validators used in prior research [8,16]. Security analyses show prompt‑injection is a real threat to LLM pipelines and motivate verifier or filtering layers [9]. Our study builds on these threads by executing a sealed, preregistered, shared‑candidate comparison that isolates the validator+repair effect on existing candidates.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand: The study was preregistered as study-cand-2026-LLM-verifier-sim2real-v1 and frozen prior to execution. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Design and data: a deterministic task generator produced N_pairs = 250 intent tasks describing constrained operator intents and required command sequences. For each intent the system produced one shared initial generation using gpt-5-mini. That single initial candidate was copied into both paired episodes: baseline (accepted as‑is; no repair) and guarded (deterministic validator run; if the validator signalled a failure a single automated repair attempt was permitted). This shared_initial_candidate design means the paired contrast measures only the effect of deterministic validation+repair on the same candidate — any between‑condition differences can arise only from deterministic validation/repair steps, not from independent first‑pass sampling. Models and tooling: declared model = gpt-5-mini (provider recorded as openai_responses); deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; adapter_family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Execution contract: one initial generation per intent, ≤1 repair per episode, maximum_model_calls preregistered = 500. The pipeline recorded all prompts, model outputs, validator traces, and repair traces immutably. Scoring and inference: the validator produced a boolean verifier_pass per episode. Primary test: exact McNemar two‑sided on the paired 2×2 contingency table; 95% CI computed by the preregistered paired bootstrap percentile (10,000 resamples, seed preserved). Exclusions and contamination: preregistered rules excluded parser‑blocking syntax or detected denylist/private data; none of these exclusions occurred during execution. The full preregistration, execution manifest, raw outputs and analysis artifacts are archived and hash‑indexed in the evidence bundle.
sections.results: Execution accounting: planned_episode_count = 500 (250 pairs × 2 episodes); completed_episode_count = 500; model_calls_used = 251 (250 shared initial generations + 1 repair call). Note on provider_call fields: stage_counts reported in the execution manifest reflect internal pipeline stages (shared_initial_generation = 250; repair = 1). condition_counts in the provider audit do not indicate independent first‑pass generations per condition; they reflect stage semantics and the single repair call. Primary outcome: complete_pair_count = 250; baseline_success_count = 249 (99.6%); guarded_success_count = 250 (100.0%). Paired contingency (guarded,baseline): n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = +0.004 (0.4 percentage points). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.012] (0 – 1.2 percentage points) from 10,000 resamples with preserved seed. Repair outcomes: a single discordant pair existed; the single permitted repair converted that baseline‑fail into a guarded‑pass (repair‑conversion = 1/250). No preregistered exclusions, contamination flags, or missing pairs occurred. All reported numeric values are drawn directly from the archived analysis artifacts (paired_contingency_table.csv; condition_summary.csv) and the deterministic reconciliation manifest.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: the preregistered hypothesis expecting a substantive paired deficit (≥15 percentage points) is not supported. For the constrained, synthetic tasks studied, gpt-5-mini produced initial candidates that the deterministic validator accepted in 249/250 cases; a single automated repair converted the only failing candidate. Possible readings: (A) modern LLMs can produce mechanically valid candidates for narrowly constrained intents and synthetic topologies; (B) the validator and task generator encoded mechanically checkable properties for which LLMs already perform well; (C) the experimental scope (synthetic tasks, limited allowed fields, single validator encoding, single‑repair policy) limited observable failure mass. Threats to validity: Internal — results depend on prompt templates, declared model, and single‑repair policy; the study followed shared_initial_candidate semantics strictly, so the paired estimate isolates validator+repair effect only. Construct — the validator checks mechanically verifiable properties (syntax and prescribed workflow sequences); broader semantic correctness (protocol dynamics, performance, emergent interactions) was not assessed. External — the confirmatory run was limited to the synthetic/emulation partition of the preregistration (the preregistration also listed community and production‑like partitions as exploratory, but these were not executed in the confirmatory run). Security and adversarial concerns: adaptive prompt‑injection, retrieval‑based attacks, vendor‑specific CLI subtleties, and real production topologies were not exercised and remain open research directions. Operational implication: in similar constrained task regimes a guarded GVR pipeline may yield small marginal verifier gains because modern LLMs already produce largely validator‑consistent candidates; this must not be generalized beyond the studied regime.
sections.conclusion: We executed a sealed, preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics to quantify the verifier‑detected benefit of deterministic validation plus one automated repair on LLM‑generated network‑configuration candidates. In N=250 constrained synthetic intent tasks, initial gpt-5-mini candidates passed the deterministic validator in 249/250 cases and the guarded pipeline converted the single failing candidate; paired improvement = 0.4 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 1.2 percentage points], p = 1.0). The preregistered near‑null result implies that GVR-style guardrails may produce limited marginal verifier benefit in some tightly constrained NetOps task regimes; broader and adversarial settings require further study. All code, raw outputs, validator traces, repair traces, and analysis artifacts described are archived and hashed in the execution bundle for reproducibility and audit.

limitations: Task scope: confirmatory execution was limited to the synthetic/emulation partition described in the preregistration; community and production‑like partitions listed in the preregistration were not executed in the confirmatory run and remain exploratory.

Validator coverage: the deterministic validator checked mechanically verifiable properties (syntax, required workflow sequences); broader semantic correctness (protocol dynamics, performance, emergent behaviors) was not assessed.
Model and tooling scope: a single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and one validator implementation were used; results do not establish multi‑model or alternate‑validator generality.

Adversary and retrieval attacks: adaptive prompt‑injection, retrieval‑based attacks, vendor‑targeted exploit vectors, and heterogeneous real‑world topologies were not evaluated and remain open threats.
Repair policy: only one automated repair attempt was permitted by design; multi‑iteration repair loops, human‑in‑the‑loop escalation, or different repair templates may change outcomes.
